title: What I Believe
summary: I lay out where I stand: my theology, life philosophy, and some personal views
html:
Discourse Philosophy

I have five rules that summarize my approach to differing opinions:

  1. Everyone knows as much about their belief as you know about yours. Everyone knows as much about your belief as you know about theirs (little to nothing).
  2. Every belief is somehow reasonable, or no one would believe it.
  3. A belief system that has existed for more than 50 years has heard every rebuttal or disproof you could imagine.
  4. Nobody thinks they are wrong, or they would change their mind.
  5. Nobody lies about what they believe. Nobody lies about what they think you believe.

Obviously, with most generalizations, this list is not always literally true. But it is functionally true, and that is the key. If you approach opposing ideas through this perspective, you will often find your opponents open and easy to engage with. I find it to be the best way to approach every discussion in good faith.

Politics

Most of my political opinions are filtered through my faith. While I consider myself fairly right-wing, this is strictly because the American political Left is further from my values as a Christian, and not because I have any respect for the political Right. I'm fairly pro-international intervention, but not strictly pro- or anti-war. I am fairly pro-free market, but I think any economic system can be corrupted. My faith is the foundational point of my political beliefs, and everything else is at least somewhat flexible.

Theology

I was raised Independent Fundamental Baptist. I have qualms with the Fundamentalist movement, but I have no bitterness or spite towards them. I definitely lean heavily Independant Baptist in my theology, but if I wasn't Baptist, I'd probably be Lutheran.

One of the foundational books of my theological philosophy was Frank Turek's book I Don't Have Enough Faith to be an Atheist, which suggested that the belief system that requires the least amount of faith to accept is Christianity (in his case, Evangelical Christianity). I approach most of my religious studies through that lens with a variation on Ockham's razor, and ask "Which denomination or sect requires the least caveats or clarification to account for contradictions?"

Why Lutheran?

I am yet to study every denomination in depth, but Lutherans seem to me to have the best balance of keeping the historical teachings of the church without replacing the Word of God with man-made tradition. I have hesitation about Lutheran doctrines such as baptism saving or the real presence that keep me more satisfied with non-sacramental theology, but if those hesitations were overcome, Lutheranism seems the most straightforward alternative to me.

Why not Catholic or Orthodox?

Catholicism lives and dies on the authority of the church and the Pope. A faith that places so much weight on fallible man does not sit right with me. While I am not convinced like some of my Evangelical peers that Catholicism is anti-Christianity, I have never been convinced that it is the true form of Christianity either, especially with the number of exceptions and caveats needed to account for any evidence that contradicts papal authority, historical succession, or church doctrinal infallibility. My Catholic friends are — for now, I suppose — my mistaken brethren.

My problem with Orthodoxy is a smaller issue that I also have with Catholicism (and to some extent high-church Protestantism) — ritualism. While I believe there is a heart to serve God and worship Him in both churches, I find most liturgical practices to be performative in my experience. It was similar to my experience in Charismatic churches, believe it or not, just a lot more sober. The practices may be wildly different, but the spirit has always felt the same to me. Not a lack of God's presence, per se, but a preference for ritual emotion over substance that clouds people's views of what exactly God's presence is.

I respect the beauty of ritual, but I appreciate the simplicity of traditional low-church worship.

Non-denominationalism

I am pro-denominational, even though I am not technically a member of one. I would probably align closest with the Southern Baptist Convention on that topic. Denomination labels are useful because they tell me a lot about a church — its theology, worship style, service structure, and sometimes even minor doctrines. For that reason, I think denomination labels are a net good.

Hell, Universalism, and Christian Identity

I accept Eternal Conscious Torment for a couple reasons linked to other parts of my faith. One is the doctrine of penal substitionary atonement, which teaches that Jesus took the full punishment for my sins in my place on the cross.

Another reason is the fact that I view hell as separation from God. Our sin nature already separates us from Him and can only be resolved through Christ's death on the cross. Hell is not just a cruel punishment, but a unavoidable necessity. Our acceptation of His sacrifice is what enables us to stand alive before a holy God in Heaven without contradicting his justice and purity.

Universalism and Inclusivism

I don't accept that the Bible teaches anywhere that salvation can come from any other faith.

“Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.” John 14:6 (KJV)

I can accept a flexible form of exclusivism that allows for salvation according to the knowledge given to the person, but it is still salvation in Christ. That is, you don't need to know the gospel perfectly, but you still must accept the parts of the gospel you know in order to be saved.

Christian Identity

I know the controversy that comes with defining "Christianity" or "Christian" as terms. I know the difficulty to define what a religion is, or the social implications of a name. I've researched why sects like the LDS prefer to be called Christian. So I must be careful when I dare broach the topic, but as a Christian, I have opinions on Christianity.

The term "Christian" serves several different roles depending on who it is used with:

  1. to identify the broad religious category you identify with
  2. to state your religion
  3. to state your eternal future.

To an atheist or agnostic, there's no practical difference between a Mormon and a Presbyterian. They both want you to attend their church in Sunday and believe in their God and give money to their organization. In this case, there is no downside to accepting LDS as Christians. In matters of religious studies or apologetics, however, conflating the two as being one religion has social consequences. Frustrations arise in conversation when neither party realizes that they are not speaking the same religious dialect. Dialogue stalls. Tempers flare. And any interest in an interfaith dialogue peters out. Ignoring differences in the name of unity actually destroys unity.

And more personally for me, acknowledging Mormons as Christians implies that the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints teaches the base doctrines necessary for salvation. I do not believe this and cannot claim it. This applies to most Restoration sects that claim the name of "Christian." It is a grave theological error for me to call such faiths "Christianity" or even confirm the idea for the sake of cooperation.

So while I think obnoxiously correcting any Mormon or JW who calls himself a Christian is dumb and disrespectful, I also believe it is equally disrespectful to pretend that I do not believe they are false religions, and more crucially, that they lead to destruction in eternity.
